claim: Experimental screens have identified tens of thousands of protein-protein interactions.
source: Experimental screens have identified tens of thousands of interactions, and structural biology has provided detailed functional insight for select 3D protein complexes.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of the field, supported by established scientific knowledge about high-throughput experimental methods.

claim: Structural biology has provided detailed functional insight for select 3D protein complexes.
source: Experimental screens have identified tens of thousands of interactions, and structural biology has provided detailed functional insight for select 3D protein complexes.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of structural biology, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Analysis of correlated evolutionary sequence changes across proteins identifies residues that are close in space with sufficient accuracy to determine the three-dimensional structure of protein complexes.
source: Building on earlier work, we show that analysis of correlated evolutionary sequence changes across proteins identifies residues that are close in space with sufficient accuracy to determine the three-dimensional structure of the protein complexes.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript including blinded tests on 76 complexes.

claim: The method was evaluated in blinded tests on 76 complexes of known 3D structure.
source: We evaluate prediction performance in blinded tests on 76 complexes of known 3D structure, predict protein–protein contacts in 32 complexes of unknown structure, and demonstrate how evolutionary couplings can be used to distinguish between interacting and non-interacting protein pairs in a large complex.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by the data presented in the Results section and supplementary materials.

claim: Protein-protein contacts were predicted in 32 complexes of unknown structure.
source: We evaluate prediction performance in blinded tests on 76 complexes of known 3D structure, predict protein–protein contacts in 32 complexes of unknown structure, and demonstrate how evolutionary couplings can be used to distinguish between interacting and non-interacting protein pairs in a large complex.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by the predictions shown in Figure 5 and supplementary files.

claim: Evolutionary couplings can be used to distinguish between interacting and non-interacting protein pairs in a large complex.
source: We evaluate prediction performance in blinded tests on 76 complexes of known 3D structure, predict protein–protein contacts in 32 complexes of unknown structure, and demonstrate how evolutionary couplings can be used to distinguish between interacting and non-interacting protein pairs in a large complex.
evidence: This is demonstrated using the ATP synthase complex as shown in Figure 6.

claim: There is little or no 3D information for approximately 80% of currently known protein interactions in bacteria, yeast, or human.
source: However, there is still little, or no, 3D information for ∼80% of the currently known protein interactions in bacteria, yeast, or human, amounting to at least ∼30,000/∼6000 incompletely characterized interactions in human and Escherichia coli, respectively (Mosca et al., 2012; Rajagopala et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mosca et al., 2012; Rajagopala et al., 2014).

claim: There are at least approximately 30,000 incompletely characterized interactions in human.
source: However, there is still little, or no, 3D information for ∼80% of the currently known protein interactions in bacteria, yeast, or human, amounting to at least ∼30,000/∼6000 incompletely characterized interactions in human and Escherichia coli, respectively (Mosca et al., 2012; Rajagopala et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mosca et al., 2012; Rajagopala et al., 2014).

claim: There are at least approximately 6000 incompletely characterized interactions in Escherichia coli.
source: However, there is still little, or no, 3D information for ∼80% of the currently known protein interactions in bacteria, yeast, or human, amounting to at least ∼30,000/∼6000 incompletely characterized interactions in human and Escherichia coli, respectively (Mosca et al., 2012; Rajagopala et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mosca et al., 2012; Rajagopala et al., 2014).

claim: Evolutionary analysis of amino acid co-variation to identify close residue contacts across protein interactions was first used 20 years ago.
source: One promising computational approach is to use evolutionary analysis of amino acid co-variation to identify close residue contacts across protein interactions, which was first used 20 years ago (Gobel et al., 1994; Pazos and Valencia, 2001), and subsequently used also to identify protein interactions (Pazos et al., 1997; Pazos and Valencia, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to historical literature (Gobel et al., 1994; Pazos and Valencia, 2001).

claim: Previous approaches using local models of co-evolution are less likely to disentangle indirect and incorrect correlations from direct co-evolution.
source: These previous approaches relied on a local model of co-evolution that is less likely to disentangle indirect and therefore incorrect correlations from the direct co-evolution, as has been described in work on residue–residue interactions in single proteins (Marks et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Marks et al., 2012) and represents a comparison between methods.

claim: Reports using a global model have been successful in identifying residue interactions from evolutionary co-variation between histidine kinases and response regulators.
source: More recently, reports using a global model have been successful in identifying residue interactions from evolutionary co-variation, for instance between histidine kinases and response regulators (Burger & van Nimwegen, 2008; Skerker et al., 2008; Weigt et al., 2009), and this approach has only recently been generalized and used to predict contacts between proteins in complexes of unknown structure, in an independent effort parallel to this work (Ovchinnikov et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Burger & van Nimwegen, 2008; Skerker et al., 2008; Weigt et al., 2009).

claim: An independent effort parallel to this work has used a global model approach to predict contacts between proteins in complexes of unknown structure.
source: More recently, reports using a global model have been successful in identifying residue interactions from evolutionary co-variation, for instance between histidine kinases and response regulators (Burger & van Nimwegen, 2008; Skerker et al., 2008; Weigt et al., 2009), and this approach has only recently been generalized and used to predict contacts between proteins in complexes of unknown structure, in an independent effort parallel to this work (Ovchinnikov et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to concurrent work (Ovchinnikov et al., 2014).

claim: Evolutionary couplings between residues can be used to determine the 3D structure of individual proteins.
source: Since the recent demonstration of the use of evolutionary couplings (ECs) between residues to determine the 3D structure of individual proteins (Marks et al., 2011; Morcos et al., 2011; Aurell and Ekeberg, 2012; Jones et al., 2012; Kamisetty et al., 2013), including integral membrane proteins (Hopf et al., 2012; Nugent and Jones, 2012), we reason that an evolutionary statistical approach such as EVcouplings (Marks et al., 2011) could be used to determine co-evolved residues between proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature (Marks et al., 2011; Morcos et al., 2011; Aurell and Ekeberg, 2012; Jones et al., 2012; Kamisetty et al., 2013).

claim: Evolutionary couplings can determine the 3D structure of integral membrane proteins.
source: Since the recent demonstration of the use of evolutionary couplings (ECs) between residues to determine the 3D structure of individual proteins (Marks et al., 2011; Morcos et al., 2011; Aurell and Ekeberg, 2012; Jones et al., 2012; Kamisetty et al., 2013), including integral membrane proteins (Hopf et al., 2012; Nugent and Jones, 2012), we reason that an evolutionary statistical approach such as EVcouplings (Marks et al., 2011) could be used to determine co-evolved residues between proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hopf et al., 2012; Nugent and Jones, 2012).

claim: An evaluation set was built based on all known binary protein interactions in E. coli that have 3D structures of the complex.
source: To assess this hypothesis, we built an evaluation set based on all known binary protein interactions in E. coli that have 3D structures of the complex as recently summarized (Rajagopala et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by the data presented in the manuscript and citation to the source of interaction data (Rajagopala et al., 2014).

claim: The best models for all 15 docked complexes have interface RMSDs under 6 Å.
source: The best models for all 15 complexes docked with evolutionary couplings have interface RMSDs under 6 Å, 12/15 have the best scoring model under 4 Å and the top ranked models for 11/15 are under 5 Å backbone interface RMSD compared to a crystal or NMR structure interface.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the docking results presented in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: 12 out of 15 docked complexes have the best scoring model under 4 Å interface RMSD.
source: The best models for all 15 complexes docked with evolutionary couplings have interface RMSDs under 6 Å, 12/15 have the best scoring model under 4 Å and the top ranked models for 11/15 are under 5 Å backbone interface RMSD compared to a crystal or NMR structure interface.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the docking results presented in Table 1.

claim: The top ranked models for 11 out of 15 docked complexes are under 5 Å backbone interface RMSD compared to a crystal or NMR structure interface.
source: The best models for all 15 complexes docked with evolutionary couplings have interface RMSDs under 6 Å, 12/15 have the best scoring model under 4 Å and the top ranked models for 11/15 are under 5 Å backbone interface RMSD compared to a crystal or NMR structure interface.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the docking results presented in Table 1.

claim: Over 70% of the generated models using evolutionary couplings are close to the experimental structures of the complexes (<4 Å backbone iRMSD).
source: Over 70% of the generated models are close to the experimental structures of the complexes (<4 Å backbone iRMSD), compared to less than 0.5% in the controls (and these were not high–ranked) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 3, 'Supplementary data').
evidence: This claim is supported by the docking results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Less than 0.5% of control models without evolutionary couplings are close to experimental structures (<4 Å backbone iRMSD).
source: Over 70% of the generated models are close to the experimental structures of the complexes (<4 Å backbone iRMSD), compared to less than 0.5% in the controls (and these were not high–ranked) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 3, 'Supplementary data').
evidence: This claim is supported by the control docking results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ribosomal proteins RS3 and RS14 have 11 true positive inter-protein ECs.
source: For example, the ribosomal proteins RS3 and RS14 have 11 true positive inter-protein ECs and result in a top ranked model only 1.1 Å iRMSD from the reference structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Table 1 and the evaluation results.

claim: The top ranked model for RS3 and RS14 is only 1.1 Å iRMSD from the reference structure.
source: For example, the ribosomal proteins RS3 and RS14 have 11 true positive inter-protein ECs and result in a top ranked model only 1.1 Å iRMSD from the reference structure.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the docking results in Table 1.

claim: Ubiquinol oxidase has 6 out of 11 true positive inter-protein contacts.
source: More surprisingly, other complexes with a lower proportion of true positive inter-protein contacts, such as Ubiquinol oxidase (6 out of 11) or the epsilon and gamma subunits of ATP synthase (8 out of 15) also produced accurate predicted complexes, with an iRMSD of 1.8 and 1.4 Å respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by the evaluation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The top ranked model for Ubiquinol oxidase has an iRMSD of 1.8 Å.
source: More surprisingly, other complexes with a lower proportion of true positive inter-protein contacts, such as Ubiquinol oxidase (6 out of 11) or the epsilon and gamma subunits of ATP synthase (8 out of 15) also produced accurate predicted complexes, with an iRMSD of 1.8 and 1.4 Å respectively.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the docking results in Table 1.

claim: The epsilon and gamma subunits of ATP synthase have 8 out of 15 true positive inter-protein contacts.
source: More surprisingly, other complexes with a lower proportion of true positive inter-protein contacts, such as Ubiquinol oxidase (6 out of 11) or the epsilon and gamma subunits of ATP synthase (8 out of 15) also produced accurate predicted complexes, with an iRMSD of 1.8 and 1.4 Å respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by the evaluation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The top ranked model for the epsilon and gamma subunits of ATP synthase has an iRMSD of 1.4 Å.
source: More surprisingly, other complexes with a lower proportion of true positive inter-protein contacts, such as Ubiquinol oxidase (6 out of 11) or the epsilon and gamma subunits of ATP synthase (8 out of 15) also produced accurate predicted complexes, with an iRMSD of 1.8 and 1.4 Å respectively.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the docking results in Table 1.

claim: Inter-protein evolutionary couplings can be sufficient to give accurate 3D models of protein complexes even in the presence of incorrect predictions.
source: The docking experiments therefore demonstrate that inter-protein ECs, even in the presence of incorrect predictions, can be sufficient to give accurate 3D models of protein complexes, but more work will be needed to quantify the likelihood of successful docking from the predicted contacts.
evidence: This claim is supported by the docking results showing accurate models despite some false positive predictions.

claim: The top 10 inter-EC pairs between MetI and MetN are accurate to within 8 Å in the MetNI complex.
source: The top 10 inter-EC pairs between MetI and MetN are accurate to within 8 Å in the MetNI complex (PDB: 3tui [Johnson et al., 2012]), resulting in an average 1.4 Å iRMSD from the crystal structure for all 100 computed 3D models (Table 1, Supplementary file 3 and 'Supplementary data').
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to the crystal structure (PDB: 3tui) and docking results.

claim: All 100 computed 3D models of MetNI have an average 1.4 Å iRMSD from the crystal structure.
source: The top 10 inter-EC pairs between MetI and MetN are accurate to within 8 Å in the MetNI complex (PDB: 3tui [Johnson et al., 2012]), resulting in an average 1.4 Å iRMSD from the crystal structure for all 100 computed 3D models (Table 1, Supplementary file 3 and 'Supplementary data').
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the docking results in Table 1.

claim: The top 3 inter-EC residue pairs between MetI and MetN constitute a residue network coupling the ATP-binding pocket of MetN to the membrane transporter MetI.
source: The top 3 inter-EC residue pairs (K136-E108, A128-L105, and E74-R124, MetI-MetN respectively) constitute a residue network coupling the ATP-binding pocket of MetN to the membrane transporter MetI.
evidence: This claim is supported by the evolutionary coupling analysis and structural interpretation shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The residue network calculated from the sequence alignment corresponds to residues identified experimentally that couple ATP hydrolysis to the open and closed conformations of the MetI dimer.
source: This network calculated from the sequence alignment corresponds to residues identified experimentally that couple ATP hydrolysis to the open and closed conformations of the MetI dimer (Johnson et al., 2012) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to experimental results cited from Johnson et al., 2012.

claim: The top 5 inter-ECs between BtuC and BtuD co-locate the L-loop of BtuC close to the Q-loop ATP-binding domain of the ATPase.
source: The top 5 inter-ECs co-locate the L-loop of BtuC close to the Q-loop ATP-binding domain of the ATPase, hence coupling the transporter with the ATP hydrolysis state in an analogous way to MetI-MetN.
evidence: This claim is supported by the evolutionary coupling analysis and structural interpretation.

claim: EVcomplex identifies not only residues close in space, but also particular pairs that are constrained by the transporter function of these complexes.
source: The identification of these coupled residues across the different subunits suggests that EVcomplex identifies not only residues close in space, but also particular pairs that are constrained by the transporter function of these complexes (Kadaba et al., 2008; Johnson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that predicted contacts correspond to functionally important residues, supported by citations.

claim: The ATP synthase ε subunit can take different positions relative to the γ subunit, executing the auto-inhibition of the enzyme by dramatic conformational changes.
source: The ATP synthase ε and γ subunit complex provides a challenge to our approach, since the ε subunit can take different positions relative to the γ subunit, executing the auto-inhibition of the enzyme by dramatic conformational changes (Cingolani and Duncan, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Cingolani and Duncan, 2011).

claim: EVcomplex accurately predicts 6 of the top 10 inter-EC pairs for the ATP synthase ε and γ subunit complex within 8 Å in the crystal structure.
source: EVcomplex accurately predicts 6 of the top 10 inter-EC pairs (within 8 Å in the crystal structure 1fs0 (Rodgers and Wilce, 2000) or 3oaa (Cingolani and Duncan, 2011)), with the top 2 inter-ECs εA45-γL215 and εA40-γL207 providing contact between the subunits along an inter-protein beta sheet.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to crystal structures (PDB: 1fs0, 3oaa).

claim: Docking with the top inter-ECs for ATP synthase ε and γ subunits results in models with 1.4 Å backbone iRMSDs to the crystal structure for the interface.
source: Docking with the top inter-ECs results in models with 1.4 Å backbone iRMSDs to the crystal structure for the interface between the N-terminal domain of the ε subunit and the γ subunit (Table 1, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the docking results in Table 1.

claim: 82 protein complexes with unknown 3D structure of the interaction that satisfy the conditions for the current approach were predicted using EVcomplex.
source: A total of 82 protein complexes with unknown 3D structure of the interaction that satisfy the conditions for the current approach, i.e., have sufficient sequences and are close in all genomes, were predicted using EVcomplex (all residue–residue inter-protein evolutionary couplings scores are available in 'Supplementary data').
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by the data presented in supplementary materials.

claim: 32 of the 82 predicted complexes have high EVcomplex scores with at least one predicted contact.
source: A total of 82 protein complexes with unknown 3D structure of the interaction that satisfy the conditions for the current approach, i.e., have sufficient sequences and are close in all genomes, were predicted using EVcomplex (all residue–residue inter-protein evolutionary couplings scores are available in 'Supplementary data'). 32 of these have high EVcomplex scores with at least one predicted contact (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and 2, and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the predictions shown in Figure 5 and supplementary files.

claim: Protein complexes with more high-scoring ECs have a higher proportion of true positives.
source: Analysis of the inter-EC predictions for known 3D complex structures shows that protein pairs with more high-scoring ECs (EVcomplex score ≥0.8) have a higher proportion of true positives (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The top 15 inter-ECs between MetQ and MetI are from one interface of MetQ to the MetI periplasmic loops, or the periplasmic end of the helices.
source: The top 15 inter-ECs between MetQ and MetI are from one interface of MetQ to the MetI periplasmic loops, or the periplasmic end of the helices, consistent with the known binding of MetQ to MetI in the periplasm.
evidence: This claim is supported by the evolutionary coupling predictions and is consistent with known biological knowledge about the system.

claim: The UmuD and UmuC complex is induced in the stress/SOS response facilitating the cleavage of UmuD to UmuD'.
source: The UmuD and UmuC complex is induced in the stress/SOS response facilitating the cleavage of UmuD to UmuD' (between C24 and G25) to form UmuD'2 which then interacts with UmuC (DNA polymerase V) in order to copy damaged DNA (Beuning et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Beuning et al., 2006).

claim: UmuD is cleaved between C24 and G25 to form UmuD'.
source: The UmuD and UmuC complex is induced in the stress/SOS response facilitating the cleavage of UmuD to UmuD' (between C24 and G25) to form UmuD'2 which then interacts with UmuC (DNA polymerase V) in order to copy damaged DNA (Beuning et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Beuning et al., 2006).

claim: UmuD'2 interacts with UmuC (DNA polymerase V) in order to copy damaged DNA.
source: The UmuD and UmuC complex is induced in the stress/SOS response facilitating the cleavage of UmuD to UmuD' (between C24 and G25) to form UmuD'2 which then interacts with UmuC (DNA polymerase V) in order to copy damaged DNA (Beuning et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Beuning et al., 2006).

claim: For 6 out of 7 ECs above the score threshold for UmuD-UmuC, residues in UmuD predicted to interface with UmuC are co-located on one face of the dimer.
source: For 6/7 ECs above the score threshold, residues in UmuD predicted to interface with UmuC are co-located on one face of the dimer.
evidence: This claim is supported by the evolutionary coupling predictions and structural analysis.

claim: Two residues (Y33, I38) in the N-terminal arm of UmuD may become available for binding UmuC after cleavage of the 24 N-terminal amino acids.
source: Two residues (Y33, I38) are located in the N-terminal arm of UmuD that, after cleavage of the 24 N-terminal amino acids, may become available for binding UmuC.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the location of predicted contacts and known biology of the system.

claim: The inter-ECs from the UmuD arm to UmuC may identify the critical residues for translesion synthesis function.
source: Since UmuD switches functions after this cleavage and can then bind UmuC, these inter-ECs may identify the critical residues for translesion synthesis function (Beuning et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the predicted contacts and known function, supported by citation.

claim: The 3D structure of the DinJ–YafQ complex was published while this manuscript was in review.
source: Whilst this manuscript was in review, the 3D structure of the previously unsolved biofilm toxin/antitoxin DinJ–YafQ complex was published (PDB: 3mlo (Liang et al., 2014)), showing the intertwining of subunits in a heterotetrameric complex.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the timing of a publication, supported by citation.

claim: 17 out of 19 predicted EC residue pairs for DinJ–YafQ are within 8 Å in the published 3D structure.
source: Whilst this manuscript was in review, the 3D structure of the previously unsolved biofilm toxin/antitoxin DinJ–YafQ complex was published (PDB: 3mlo (Liang et al., 2014)), showing the intertwining of subunits in a heterotetrameric complex. 17/19 predicted EC residue pairs are within 8 Å in this 3D structure (Supplementary file 4 and 'Supplementary data').
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to the published structure (PDB: 3mlo).

claim: EVcomplex can be used to reveal 3D structural details of yet unsolved protein complexes given sufficient evolutionary information.
source: In general, the agreement between our de novo predicted inter-protein ECs and available experimental data serves as a measure of confidence for the predicted residue pair interactions and suggests that EVcomplex can be used to reveal 3D structural details of yet unsolved protein complexes given sufficient evolutionary information.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the validation of predictions against experimental data.

claim: Evolutionary couplings were calculated for all 28 possible pair combinations of different ATP synthase subunits.
source: As a demonstration exercise, we calculated evolutionary couplings for all 28 possible pair combinations of different ATP synthase subunits (centered around the E. coli ATP synthase) and transformed the ECs into EVcomplex scores for all inter-protein residue pairs (experimentally determined stoichiometry: α3β3γδεab2c10, Supplementary file 5 and 'Supplementary data').
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by the data presented in supplementary materials.

claim: Using the default EVcomplex score threshold of 0.8, 24 of the 28 possible interactions between ATP synthase subunits are correctly classified as interacting or non-interacting.
source: Using the default EVcomplex score threshold of 0.8 to discriminate between interacting and non-interacting pairs of subunits, 24 of the 28 possible interactions between the subunits are correctly classified as interacting or non-interacting.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Four interactions (ε and c, γ and c, ε and β, b and β) are not identified as interacting using the 0.8 EVcomplex threshold.
source: The four incorrect predictions (namely: ε and c, γ and c, ε and β, b and β, for which there is some experimental evidence) are not identified as interacting using the 0.8 EVcomplex threshold.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 80% of the interacting residue pairs in the known 3D structure parts of the ATP synthase complex are correctly predicted.
source: In total 80% of the interacting residue pairs in the known 3D structure parts of the synthase complex (7 pairs of subunits) are correctly predicted (threshold: 10 Å minimum atom distance between two residues).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of ATP synthase predictions.

claim: The EVcomplex method has potential in helping to elucidate protein–protein interaction networks from evolutionary sequence co-variation.
source: This exercise of predicting the presence or absence of interaction between any two proteins indicates the potential of the EVcomplex method in helping to elucidate protein–protein interaction networks from evolutionary sequence co-variation and identify interacting subunits of large macromolecular complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the successful prediction of interactions in the ATP synthase complex.

claim: The a- and b- subunits of E. coli ATP synthase are known to interact, but the monomer structure of subunits a and b and the structure of their interaction in the complex are unknown.
source: The a- and b- subunits of E. coli ATP synthase are known to interact, but the monomer structure of subunits a and b and the structure of their interaction in the complex are unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There are no experimentally determined atomic resolution structures of the a-subunit of ATP synthase.
source: To our knowledge, there are no experimentally determined atomic resolution structures of the a-subunit of ATP synthase.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: A 3D model of the a-subunit from 1999 was computed using five helical–helical interactions inferred from second suppressor mutation experiments.
source: A 3D model of the a-subunit is from 1999 (1c17(Rastogi and Girvin, 1999)) and was computed using five helical–helical interactions that were inferred from second suppressor mutation experiments, and then imposed as distance restraints for TMH2-5, revealing a four helical bundle (with no information for TMH1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Rastogi and Girvin, 1999).

claim: Cross-linking experiments identified contacting residues from all pairs of helical combinations of TM2-TM5 in the a-subunit.
source: Later, cross-linking experiments (Schwem and Fillingame, 2006) identified contacting residues from all pairs of helical combinations of TM2-TM5 (6 pairs), supporting the earlier 4 helical bundle topology.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Schwem and Fillingame, 2006).

claim: 7 of the 8 cross-linked pairs in the a-subunit are either exactly the same pair or adjacent to many pairs in the top L intra a-subunit evolutionary couplings.
source: 7 of the 8 cross-linked pairs are either exactly the same pair (L120-I246) or adjacent to many pairs in the top L intra a-subunit evolutionary couplings (ECs).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of predicted ECs to experimental crosslinking data.

claim: The helix packing arrangement in the predicted structure of the a-subunit is consistent with the topology suggested on the basis of crosslinking studies.
source: In fact, the helix packing arrangement in the predicted structure of the a-subunit is consistent with the topology suggested on the basis of crosslinking studies (Long et al., 2002; DeLeon-Rangel et al., 2003; Fillingame and Steed, 2014), including the lack of contacts for transmembrane helix 1 with the other 4 helices ('Supplementary data').
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to experimental crosslinking studies cited in the text.

claim: The top inter-protein EC pair between subunits a and b (aK74–bE34) coincides with experimental crosslinking evidence.
source: The top inter-protein EC pair between subunits a and b, aK74–bE34, coincides with experimental crosslinking evidence of the interaction of aK74 with the b-subunit and the position of E34 of the b subunit emerging from the membrane on the cytoplasmic side (Long et al., 2002; DeLeon-Rangel et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to experimental crosslinking data cited in the text.

claim: 6 of the 13 high score ECs between a and b subunits are in the same region as the experimental crosslinks.
source: Indeed, 6 of the 13 high score ECs are in the same region as the experimental crosslinks, for instance between the cytoplasmic loop between the first two helices of the a-subunit and the b-subunit helix as it emerges from the membrane bilayer (DeLeon-Rangel et al., 2013), or between a239V in TM helix 5 and bL16 (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to experimental crosslinking data.

claim: The top EC between the a- and c-subunits (aG213 – cM65) lies close to the functionally critical aR210–cD61 interaction.
source: Additionally, the top EC between the a- and c-subunits (aG213 – cM65) lies close to the functionally critical aR210–cD61 interaction (Dmitriev et al., 1999) on the same helical faces of the respective subunits (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to known functional interactions cited in the text.

claim: A primary limitation of the current approach is its dependence on the availability of a large number of evolutionarily related sequences.
source: A primary limitation of our current approach is its dependence on the availability of a large number of evolutionarily related sequences.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the method based on the requirements for statistical analysis.

claim: If a protein interaction is conserved across enough sequenced genomes, using a single pair per genome can give accurate predictions of the interacting residues.
source: If a protein interaction is conserved across enough sequenced genomes, using a single pair per genome can give accurate predictions of the interacting residues.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the methodology and results of the study.

claim: Including multiple paralogs of the interacting proteins from each genome requires correct pairing of the interaction partners, which is in general hard to ascertain.
source: A solution to this could be to include multiple paralogs of the interacting proteins from each genome, but this requires correct pairing of the interaction partners, which is in general hard to ascertain.
evidence: This is a discussion of methodological challenges based on biological knowledge.

claim: A genome distance requirement across all genomes for all homolog pairs was imposed to be less sensitive to complications from paralog pairing.
source: Hence, in this current version of the method, we have imposed a genome distance requirement across all genomes for all homolog pairs in order to be less sensitive to these complications.
evidence: This is a methodological decision described in the manuscript.

claim: With currently available sequences (May 2014 release of the UniProt database), EVcomplex is able to provide information for about 1/10th of the known 3000 protein interactions in the E. coli genome.
source: With currently available sequences (May 2014 release of the UniProt database), EVcomplex is able to provide information for about 1/10th of the known 3000 protein interactions in the E. coli genome.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 1B showing the fraction of interactions with sufficient sequences.

claim: Once there are approximately 10,000 bacterial genome sequences of sufficient diversity, one would have enough information to test each potentially interacting pair of homologs for evidence of interaction.
source: Once there are ∼10,000 bacterial genome sequences of sufficient diversity, one would have enough information to test each potentially interacting pair of homologs for evidence of interaction and, given sufficiently strong evolutionary couplings, infer the 3D structure of each protein–protein pair, as well as of complexes with more than two proteins.
evidence: This is a projection about future capabilities based on the current results and sequence growth trends.

claim: Determining the three-dimensional models of complexes from the predicted contacts was successful in many of the tested instances.
source: Determining the three-dimensional models of complexes from the predicted contacts was successful in many of the tested instances.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the docking results presented in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: Using minimal computing resources and a small number of inter-EC-derived contacts, low interface positional RMSDs relative to experimental structures can be achieved.
source: Using minimal computing resources and a small number of inter-EC-derived contacts, low interface positional RMSDs relative to experimental structures can be achieved.
evidence: This is supported by the docking results showing accurate models with few constraints.

claim: Deconvoluting homomultimeric inter-ECs from the intra-protein signal is an important technical challenge for future work.
source: However, a significant number of proteins exist as homomultimers within larger complexes. To determine models of these complexes one must deconvolute homomultimeric inter-ECs from the intra-protein signal, which is an important technical challenge for future work.
evidence: This is a stated limitation and future direction for the method.

claim: The analysis of subunit interactions in ATP synthase is a 'proof of principle' study showing that methods such as EVcomplex can determine which proteins interact with each other.
source: The analysis of subunit interactions in ATP synthase in this work is a 'proof of principle' study showing that methods such as EVcomplex can determine which proteins interact with each other at the same time as specific residue pair couplings across the proteins (as also shown in the work by the Baker lab on ribosomal protein interactions (Ovchinnikov et al., 2014)).
evidence: This is a characterization of the ATP synthase analysis, with reference to parallel work.

claim: Understanding the networks of protein interactions is of critical interest in eukaryotic systems.
source: Understanding the networks of protein interactions is of critical interest in eukaryotic systems, such as networks of protein kinases, GPCRs, or PDZ domain proteins.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of the research area based on general scientific knowledge.

claim: Results on the two-component signaling system (histidine kinase/response regulator) suggest optimism for handling less obligate interactions.
source: Although we do not know how well our evolutionary coupling approach will handle less obligate interactions, results on the two-component signaling system (histidine kinase/response regulator) both here and in other work (Skerker et al., 2008; Weigt et al., 2009) suggest optimism.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on results from this work and cited literature.

claim: The EVcomplex score is a heuristic based on the distribution of raw EC scores from the statistical model, their dependence on sequence alignment depth and the length of the concatenated sequences.
source: The approximately scale-free EVcomplex score is a heuristic based on the distribution of raw EC scores from the statistical model, their dependence on sequence alignment depth and the length of the concatenated sequences.
evidence: This is a description of the EVcomplex score methodology.

claim: The EVcomplex score provides a simple way of accounting for dependencies such that a uniform threshold can be used for any protein pair with the expectation of reasonably accurate predictions.
source: The score provides a simple way of accounting for these dependencies such that a uniform threshold, say 0.8, can be used for any protein pair with the expectation of reasonably accurate predictions.
evidence: This is a description of the purpose and utility of the EVcomplex score.

claim: On average 74% of the predicted pairs with EVcomplex score greater than 0.8 will be accurate to within 10 Å of an experimental structure of the complex.
source: The relationship between the EVcomplex score and the precision of the corresponding inter-protein ECs suggests that on average 74% (69%) of the predicted pairs with EVcomplex score greater than 0.8 will be accurate to within 10 Å (8 Å) of an experimental structure of the complex (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: On average 69% of the predicted pairs with EVcomplex score greater than 0.8 will be accurate to within 8 Å of an experimental structure of the complex.
source: The relationship between the EVcomplex score and the precision of the corresponding inter-protein ECs suggests that on average 74% (69%) of the predicted pairs with EVcomplex score greater than 0.8 will be accurate to within 10 Å (8 Å) of an experimental structure of the complex (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Most complexes have at least one inter-protein predicted contact above the selected score threshold of 0.8 (53/76 complexes).
source: Most complexes have at least one inter-protein predicted contact above the selected score threshold of 0.8 (53/76 complexes).
evidence: This claim is supported by the evaluation results on the benchmark set.

claim: The histidine kinase and response regulator system has 78 predicted residue pairs with precision over 80%.
source: Three complexes have more than 20 predicted inter-protein residue contacts which are over 80% accurate, namely the histidine kinase and response regulator system (78 residue pairs), t-RNA synthetase (32 residue pairs), and the vitamin B importer complex (21 residue pairs), with precision over 80% (complex numbers 330, 019, 130 respectively, Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplements 3–8, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the evaluation results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The t-RNA synthetase complex has 32 predicted residue pairs with precision over 80%.
source: Three complexes have more than 20 predicted inter-protein residue contacts which are over 80% accurate, namely the histidine kinase and response regulator system (78 residue pairs), t-RNA synthetase (32 residue pairs), and the vitamin B importer complex (21 residue pairs), with precision over 80% (complex numbers 330, 019, 130 respectively, Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplements 3–8, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the evaluation results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The vitamin B importer complex has 21 predicted residue pairs with precision over 80%.
source: Three complexes have more than 20 predicted inter-protein residue contacts which are over 80% accurate, namely the histidine kinase and response regulator system (78 residue pairs), t-RNA synthetase (32 residue pairs), and the vitamin B importer complex (21 residue pairs), with precision over 80% (complex numbers 330, 019, 130 respectively, Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplements 3–8, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the evaluation results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The ethanolamine ammonia-lyase complex has 3 predicted inter-protein residue pairs above the score threshold and 5 additional correct pairs with EVcomplex scores slightly below the threshold.
source: For instance, the ethanolamine ammonia-lyase complex (complex 065) has only 3 predicted inter-protein residue pairs above the score threshold, but in fact has 5 additional correct pairs with EVcomplex scores slightly below the threshold of 0.8 which cluster with the 3 high-scoring contacts on the monomers, indicating that they are also correct.
evidence: This claim is supported by the evaluation results for this specific complex.

claim: Some high confidence inter-protein ECs in the test set are not close in 3D space when compared to their known 3D structures.
source: Some of the high confidence inter-protein ECs in the test set are not close in 3D space when compared to their known 3D structures.
evidence: This is an observation about false positives in the predictions.

claim: False positives may result from the assumption that the interaction between paired proteins is conserved across species and across paralogs.
source: These false positives may be a result of assumptions in the method that are not always correct. This includes (1) the assumption that the interaction between paired proteins is conserved across species and across paralogs, and (2) that truly co-evolved residues across proteins are indeed always close in 3D, which is not always the case.
evidence: This is a discussion of potential sources of error in the method.

claim: Complexes may exist in alternative conformations that have not necessarily all been captured yet by crystal or NMR structures.
source: In addition, the complexes may also exist in alternative conformations that have not necessarily all been captured yet by crystal or NMR structures, for instance in the case of the large conformational changes of the BtuCDF complex (Hvorup et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a discussion of potential sources of apparent false positives, supported by citation to an example.

claim: 326 interactions were identified after removing redundancy and requiring close genome distance between the pairs of proteins.
source: To assemble the broadest possible data sets to test the approach and make predictions, we take all known interacting proteins assembled in a published data set that contains ∼3500 high-confidence protein interactions in E. coli (Rajagopala et al., 2014). After removing redundancy and requiring close genome distance between the pairs of proteins this results in 326 interactions, see 'Materials and methods' (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1 and 2),
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the dataset construction, supported by reference to supplementary materials.

claim: The paired sequences are concatenated and statistical co-evolution analysis is performed using EVcouplings.
source: The paired sequences are concatenated and statistical co-evolution analysis is performed using EVcouplings (Marks et al., 2011; Morcos et al., 2011; Aurell and Ekeberg, 2012), that applies a pseudolikelihood maximization (PLM) approximation to determine the interaction parameters in the underlying maximum entropy probability model (Balakrishnan et al., 2011; Ekeberg et al., 2013; Kamisetty et al., 2013), simultaneously generating both intra- and inter-EC scores for all pairs of residues within and across the protein pairs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by citations to the methods used.

claim: EVcouplings applies a pseudolikelihood maximization (PLM) approximation to determine the interaction parameters in the underlying maximum entropy probability model.
source: The paired sequences are concatenated and statistical co-evolution analysis is performed using EVcouplings (Marks et al., 2011; Morcos et al., 2011; Aurell and Ekeberg, 2012), that applies a pseudolikelihood maximization (PLM) approximation to determine the interaction parameters in the underlying maximum entropy probability model (Balakrishnan et al., 2011; Ekeberg et al., 2013; Kamisetty et al., 2013), simultaneously generating both intra- and inter-EC scores for all pairs of residues within and across the protein pairs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by citations.

claim: Previous work has indicated that the global probability model approach requires a minimum number of sequences in the alignment with at least 1 non-redundant sequence per residue.
source: Evolutionary coupling calculations in previous work have indicated that this global probability model approach requires a minimum number of sequences in the alignment with at least 1 non-redundant sequence per residue (Marks et al., 2011; Morcos et al., 2011; Hopf et al., 2012; Jones et al., 2012; Kamisetty et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The current approach allows complexes with fewer available sequences to be assessed (minimum at 0.3 non-redundant sequences per residue).
source: Our current approach allows complexes with fewer available sequences to be assessed (minimum at 0.3 non-redundant sequences per residue) by using a new quality assessment score to assess the likelihood of the predicted contacts to be correct.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about an improvement in the current work.

claim: Most pairs of residues are not coupled and true pair couplings are outliers in the high-scoring tail of the distribution.
source: The EVcomplex score is based on the knowledge that most pairs of residues are not coupled and true pair couplings are outliers in the high-scoring tail of the distribution (See 'Materials and methods', Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a description of the basis for the EVcomplex score, supported by figures.

claim: If the number of sequences per residue is not controlled for, there is a large bias in the results, overestimating performance with low numbers of sequences.
source: If the number of sequences per residue is not controlled for, there is a large bias in the results, overestimating performance with low numbers of sequences (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The precise functional form of the correction for low numbers of sequences was chosen non-blindly after observing the dependencies in the test set.
source: The precise functional form of the correction for low numbers of sequences was chosen non-blindly after observing the dependencies in the test set.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about how the EVcomplex score was developed.

claim: Each protein from all pairs in the dataset was used to generate a multiple sequence alignment using jackhmmer to search the UniProt database with 5 iterations.
source: Each protein from all pairs in our data set was used to generate a multiple sequence alignment (MSA) using jackhmmer (Johnson et al., 2010) to search the UniProt database (UniProt Consortium, 2014) with 5 iterations.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the alignment generation process.

claim: A bit score threshold of 0.5 * monomer sequence length was chosen as homolog inclusion criterion.
source: To obtain alignments of consistent evolutionary depths across all the proteins, a bit score threshold of 0.5 * monomer sequence length was chosen as homolog inclusion criterion (-incdomT parameter), rather than a fixed E-value threshold which selects for different degrees of evolutionary divergence based on the length of the input sequence.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the alignment parameters.

claim: Proteins in close proximity on the genome are more likely to interact.
source: Here, we assume that proteins in close proximity on the genome, e.g., on the same operon, are more likely to interact, as in the methods used previously matching histidine kinase and response regulator interacting pairs (Skerker et al., 2008; Weigt et al., 2009) ('Supplementary data').
evidence: This is an assumption of the method, supported by citations to previous work using similar assumptions.

claim: Genomic locations of proteins in the alignments were retrieved and pairs were concatenated following 2 rules: the CDS of each concatenated protein pair must be located on the same genomic contig and each pair must be the closest to one another on the genome.
source: We retrieved the genomic locations of proteins in the alignments and concatenated pairs following 2 rules: (i) the CDS of each concatenated protein pair must be located on the same genomic contig (using ENA (Pakseresht et al., 2014) for mapping) and (ii) each pair must be the closest to one another on the genome, when compared to all other possible pairings in the same species.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the sequence pairing procedure.

claim: Concatenated sequence pairs were filtered based on the distribution of genomic distances to exclude outlier pairs with high genomic distances of more than 10k nucleotides.
source: The concatenated sequence pairs were filtered based on the distribution of genomic distances to exclude outlier pairs with high genomic distances of more than 10k nucleotides ('Supplementary data').
evidence: This is a methodological description of the filtering procedure.

claim: Alignment members were clustered together and reweighted if 80% or more of their residues were identical.
source: Alignment members were clustered together and reweighted if 80% or more of their residues were identical (thus implicitly removing duplicate sequences from the alignment).
evidence: This is a methodological description of the sequence redundancy reduction procedure.

claim: Inter- and intra-ECs were calculated on the alignment of concatenated sequences using a global probability model of sequence co-evolution.
source: Inter- and intra-ECs were calculated on the alignment of concatenated sequences using a global probability model of sequence co-evolution, adapted from the method for single proteins (Marks et al., 2011; Morcos et al., 2011; Hopf et al., 2012) using a pseudo-likelihood maximization (PLM) (Balakrishnan et al., 2011; Ekeberg et al., 2013) rather than mean field approximation to calculate the coupling parameters.
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by citations.

claim: Columns in the alignment that contain more than 80% gaps were excluded.
source: Columns in the alignment that contain more than 80% gaps were excluded and the weight of each sequence was adjusted to represent its cluster size in the alignment thus reducing the influence of identical or near-identical sequences in the calculation.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the alignment processing.

claim: The weight of each sequence was adjusted to represent its cluster size in the alignment.
source: Columns in the alignment that contain more than 80% gaps were excluded and the weight of each sequence was adjusted to represent its cluster size in the alignment thus reducing the influence of identical or near-identical sequences in the calculation.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the sequence weighting procedure.

claim: The background distribution of EC scores between non-coupled positions is approximately symmetric around a zero mean.
source: In order to estimate the accuracy of the EC prediction, we evaluate the calculated inter-ECs based on the following observations: (1) most pairs of positions in an alignment are not coupled, i.e., have an EC score close to zero, and tend to be distant in the 3D structure; (2) the background distribution of EC scores between non-coupled positions is approximately symmetric around a zero mean; and (3) higher-scoring positive score outliers capture 3D proximity more accurately than lower-scoring outliers (See also Figure 2).
evidence: This is an observation about the properties of EC score distributions used to develop the EVcomplex score.

claim: Higher-scoring positive score outliers capture 3D proximity more accurately than lower-scoring outliers.
source: In order to estimate the accuracy of the EC prediction, we evaluate the calculated inter-ECs based on the following observations: (1) most pairs of positions in an alignment are not coupled, i.e., have an EC score close to zero, and tend to be distant in the 3D structure; (2) the background distribution of EC scores between non-coupled positions is approximately symmetric around a zero mean; and (3) higher-scoring positive score outliers capture 3D proximity more accurately than lower-scoring outliers (See also Figure 2).
evidence: This is an observation about the properties of EC scores used to develop the EVcomplex score.

claim: The width of the background distribution can be approximated using the absolute value of the minimal inter-EC score.
source: The width of the (symmetric) background EC score distribution can be approximated using the absolute value of the minimal inter-EC score.
evidence: This is a methodological description of how the background noise is estimated.

claim: Individual monomer models were built de novo for the structurally unsolved a-subunit of ATP synthase and UmuC using the EVfold pipeline.
source: To interpret the EVcomplex prediction of interaction between subunits a and b of the ATP synthase as well as UmuC and UmuD, individual monomer models were built de novo for the structurally unsolved a-subunit of ATP synthase and UmuC using the EVfold pipeline as previously published (Marks et al., 2011; Hopf et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by citations to the EVfold method.

claim: A diverse set of 15 complexes was chosen from the 22 in the evaluation set that had at least 5 couplings above a complex score of 0.8 and was subsequently docked.
source: A diverse set of 15 complexes was chosen from the 22 in the evaluation set that had at least 5 couplings above a complex score of 0.8 and was subsequently docked (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a methodological description of the docking test set selection.

claim: Where possible, complexes that had a solved 3D structure of the unbound monomer were used for docking.
source: Proteins that have been crystallized together in a complex could bias the results of the docking, as they have complementary positions of the surface side chains. Therefore, where possible we used complexes that had a solved 3D structure of the unbound monomer, namely GcsH/GcsT, CyoA, FimC, DhaL, AtpE, PtqA/PtqB, RS10, and HK/RR, and in all other cases the side chains of the monomers were randomized either by using SCWRL4 (Krivov et al., 2009) or restrained minimization with Schrodinger Protein Preparation Wizard (Sastry et al., 2013) before docking.
evidence: This is a methodological description of how structures were prepared for docking to avoid bias.

claim: HADDOCK was used to dock the monomers for each protein pair with all inter-ECs with an EVcomplex score of 0.8 or above implemented as distance restraints.
source: We used HADDOCK (Dominguez et al., 2003), a widely used docking program based on ARIA (Linge et al., 2003) and the CNS software (Brunger, 2007) (Crystallography and NMR System), to dock the monomers for each protein pair with all inter-ECs with an EVcomplex score of 0.8 or above implemented as distance restraints on the α-carbon atoms of the backbone.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the docking procedure, supported by citations.

claim: Each docking calculation starts with a rigid-body energy minimization, followed by semi-flexible refinement in torsion angle space, and ends with further refinement of the models in explicit solvent.
source: Each docking calculation starts with a rigid-body energy minimization, followed by semi-flexible refinement in torsion angle space, and ends with further refinement of the models in explicit solvent (water). 500/100/100 models generated for each of the 3 steps, respectively.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the HADDOCK docking protocol.

claim: As a negative control, each protein complex was also docked using center of mass restraints alone.
source: As a negative control, each protein complex was also docked using center of mass restraints alone (ab initio docking mode of HADDOCK) (de Vries et al., 2007) and in this case generating 10,000/500/500 models.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the control experiments.

claim: Each of the generated models is scored using a weighted sum of electrostatic and van der Waals energies complemented by an empirical desolvation energy term.
source: Each of the generated models is scored using a weighted sum of electrostatic (Eelec) and van der Waals (Evdw) energies complemented by an empirical desolvation energy term (Edesolv) (Fernandez-Recio et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a methodological description of the model scoring, supported by citation.

claim: All computed models in the docked set were compared to the cognate crystal structures by the RMSD of all backbone atoms at the interface of the complex using ProFit v.3.1.
source: All computed models in the docked set were compared to the cognate crystal structures by the RMSD of all backbone atoms at the interface of the complex using ProFit v.3.1 (http://www.bioinf.org.uk/software/profit/).
evidence: This is a methodological description of how model accuracy was assessed.

claim: The interface is defined as the set of all residues that contain any atom <6 Å away from any atom of the complex partner.
source: The interface is defined as the set of all residues that contain any atom <6 Å away from any atom of the complex partner.
evidence: This is a methodological definition used in the analysis.
